extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (educational institutions), school administrators, Title IX coordinators, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble to final Title IX regulations explaining definitions (recipient, student, party, sex discrimination) and §106.11 application rules on when and how a recipient must address sex-based harassment and hostile environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of 'education program or activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'education program or activity' is not separately defined in Title IX statute or regulations for all recipients; a fact-specific inquiry is required to determine whether a particular program or activity of a non-educational institution recipient is educational and thus covered by Title IX. If any part of an educational institution receives Federal funds, all of its operations are covered by Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the statutory/regulatory text does not separately define the term for all contexts, recipients must analyze facts to determine coverage. Court decisions (e.g., O'Connor v. Davis; Horner; Cohen v. Brown Univ.) support the broad application where portions of an institution receive federal funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'recipient'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'recipient' includes entities that receive Federal financial assistance, whether directly or through an intermediary; that definition reaches entities such as charter school operating companies and subcontractors who receive Federal funds through a contract with a funding recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to amend §106.2 because courts (e.g., Peltier; citing NCAA v. Smith) have interpreted the longstanding regulatory definition to include entities receiving assistance through intermediaries. Recipients should therefore treat contractors/subcontractors and operating companies as potentially subject to Title IX when they receive federal assistance directly or indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'student'
rubrics_metrics.description: The longstanding regulatory definition of 'student' is 'a person who has gained admission.' This includes applicants who have gained admission and need not be limited to formally enrolled students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must notify persons who have gained admission of nondiscrimination policies and resolve student complaints. 'Admission' as defined in §106.2 covers selection for part-time, full-time, special, associate, transfer, exchange, or any other enrollment, membership, or matriculation in or at an education program or activity. The Department rejects concerns that this is overly burdensome and explains differences with FERPA and the Clery Act. The definition is intended to ensure applicants and admitted persons attempting to participate in programs have access to Title IX protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'party'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'party' or 'parties' in the final regulations is intended to include only a 'complainant' or 'respondent' as defined in §106.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'party' does not include a Title IX Coordinator who initiates a complaint under §106.44(f)(1)(v) or other participants in Title IX grievance procedures such as witnesses or adjudicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to add a separate definition of 'sex discrimination'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department determined not to add a standalone regulatory definition of 'sex discrimination'; instead, final §106.10 and other sections (including §106.31) clarify the scope and provide examples of prohibited sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where clarification is needed, recipients should consult §106.10 and the examples elsewhere in the regulations (e.g., §106.31) rather than expect a single statutory definition in §106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of §106.11 — conduct occurring under a recipient's education program or activity
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.11 requires a recipient to address sex-based harassment that occurs 'under' its education program or activity broadly—on the recipient's grounds, during school activities off campus, and under a recipient's disciplinary authority; Title IX applies to both in-person and online conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final §106.11 covers conduct in buildings owned or controlled by student organizations officially recognized by a postsecondary institution; conduct subject to a recipient's disciplinary authority that occurs off campus; conduct via school-sponsored electronic devices, networks, and digital platforms (including AI technologies); field trips, online classes, athletic programs, and training programs sponsored by a recipient. The list is illustrative, not exhaustive, and application depends on facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient responsibility limited by disciplinary authority and substantial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent with Davis and the final §106.11, a recipient is responsible only for alleged discriminatory conduct that occurs under its education program or activity — i.e., in a 'context' over which the recipient has substantial control or disciplinary authority; the recipient is not responsible for actions of parties over which it lacks significant control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing obligations, recipients should focus on whether they exercise disciplinary authority over the respondent and the context in which the conduct occurred, rather than solely on whether conduct occurred 'on' or 'off' campus. Courts (e.g., Davis; Brown) inform this substantial-control analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to address hostile environments under the recipient's program or activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must address a sex-based hostile environment that exists under its education program or activity in the United States, even when some conduct alleged to be contributing to that hostile environment occurred outside the recipient's program or activity or outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department replaced phrasing in §106.11 to 'even when some conduct alleged to be contributing to the hostile environment' to clarify that conduct contributing to a hostile environment need not itself be 'sex-based harassment.' The recipient's obligation is limited to addressing the hostile environment that exists under its program or activity; it is not required to respond independently to every outside incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for evaluating whether a sex-based hostile environment exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating the totality of the circumstances, a recipient must consider: (1) the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the recipient's education program or activity; (2) the type, frequency, and duration of the conduct; (3) the parties' ages, roles within the recipient's education program or activity, previous interactions, and other factors about each party relevant to effects of the conduct; (4) the location of the conduct and the context in which the conduct occurred; and (5) other sex-based harassment in the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all alleged conduct occurring outside a recipient's program or activity will contribute to a hostile environment. The totality of circumstances analysis is fact-specific and must be applied to determine whether a hostile environment exists under the recipient's program or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on responding to off-campus conduct and availability of supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is not required under Title IX to provide supportive measures or to investigate off-campus sex-based harassment that has not contributed to a sex-based hostile environment under its program or activity, although it may choose to provide support. If a recipient has information indicating a specific and imminent threat within its program or activity, it must take reasonable action (e.g., issuing a no-trespass order or notifying law enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the preamble (Student A/Student B; Student C) illustrate that while recipients must address resultant hostile environments on campus, they do not have a standalone obligation under Title IX to address the underlying off-campus incident that does not contribute to an on-campus hostile environment. Recipients may still take discretionary supportive actions such as counseling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with law enforcement and mandatory reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the regulations prevents a complainant from reporting alleged sex-based harassment to law enforcement, and mandatory reporting laws may require a recipient to report incidents to law enforcement in addition to Title IX obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How a recipient's Title IX grievance procedures interact with a concurrent law enforcement proceeding is fact-specific and depends on applicable procedures, particulars of the conduct, and local laws. Recipients should coordinate responses where appropriate while respecting legal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraterritorial limitation of Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX does not apply extraterritorially; the statute's plain text restricts application to 'No person in the United States,' and the Department declines to adopt language extending Title IX to conduct occurring outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Title IX does not apply to conduct outside the United States (including study abroad programs), a recipient may consider conduct that occurred abroad when determining whether a hostile environment exists in its U.S.-based program or activity (i.e., if the foreign conduct contributes to an on-campus hostile environment). Recipients may also address conduct occurring abroad through their own codes of conduct or policies even though Title IX does not impose that obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of third-party assailants and 'representatives' of recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: If an assailant is a third party over whom the recipient does not exercise disciplinary authority (i.e., not a 'person over whom the recipient exercises disciplinary authority'), the sexual assault did not occur within the recipient's education program or activity for Title IX purposes; however, recipients retain the ability to take measures such as issuing a no-trespass order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies it did not intend to create a new 'representative' concept; rather, the relevant inquiry is whether the recipient exercises disciplinary authority over the alleged perpetrator. Even when Title IX does not require action against a third party, recipients may take reasonable steps to protect students.
